paragraphs.text: Commentary § 6.30:1 Rule 6.30 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 6.30. Test for a Restricted Access Order In Chemtrade Electrochem Inc. v. Stikeman Elliott LLP, 2019 ABQB 562, 2019 CarswellAlta 1503, 38 C.P.C. (8th) 71, Associate Chief Justice Rooke said: [13] The test for obtaining an order restricting access to a court file is set out in Sierra Club of Canada v Canada (Minister of Finance), 2002 SCC 41 (CanLII), at para.53: (a) such an order is necessary in order to prevent a serious risk to an important interest, including a commercial interest, in the context of litigation because reasonably alternative measures will not prevent the risk; and (b) the salutary effects of the confidentiality order, including the effects on the right of civil litigants to a fair trial, outweigh its deleterious effects, including the effects on the right to free expression, which in this context includes the public interest in open and accessible court proceedings. [Emphasis added.] An appeal of Associate Chief Justice Rooke's order was dismissed (see: Chemtrade Electrochem Inc. v. Stikeman Elliott LLP, 2020 ABCA 322, 2020 CarswellAlta 1630. In Toronto Star Newspapers Ltd. v. Ontario, 2005 SCC 41, 2005 CarswellOnt 2613, 2005 CarswellOnt 2614, EYB 2005-92055, [2005] 2 S.C.R. 188, 76 O.R. (3d) 320 (note), 197 C.C.C. (3d) 1, 29 C.R. (6th) 251, 253 D.L.R. (4th) 577, 132 C.R.R. (2d) 178, (sub nom. R. v. Toronto Star Newspapers Ltd., 335 N.R. 201, 200 O.A.C. 348, [2005] S.C.J. No. 41, Justice Fish said: 1 In any constitutional climate, the administration of justice thrives on exposure to light—and withers under a cloud of secrecy. 2 That lesson of history is enshrined in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Section 2(b) of the Charter guarantees, in more comprehensive terms, freedom of communication and freedom of expression. These fundamental and closely related freedoms both depend for their vitality on public access to information of public interest. What goes on in the courts ought therefore to be, and manifestly is, of central concern to Canadians. 3 The freedoms I have mentioned, though fundamental, are by no means absolute. Under certain conditions, public access to confidential or sensitive information related to court proceedings will endanger and not protect the integrity of our system of justice. A temporary shield will in some cases suffice; in others, permanent protection is warranted. 4 Competing claims related to court proceedings necessarily involve an exercise in judicial discretion. It is now well established that court proceedings are presumptively “open” in Canada. Public access will be barred only when the appropriate court, in the exercise of its discretion, concludes that disclosure would subvert the ends of justice or unduly impair its proper administration. 5 This criterion has come to be known as the Dagenais/Mentuck test, after the decisions of this Court in which the governing principles were established and refined. The issue in this case is whether that test, developed in the context of publication bans at the time of trial, applies as well at the pre-charge or “investigative stage” of criminal proceedings. More particularly, whether it applies to “sealing orders” concerning search warrants and the informations upon which their issuance was judicially authorized. 6 The Court of Appeal for Ontario held that it does and the Crown now appeals against that decision. 7 I would dismiss the appeal. In my view, the Dagenais/Mentuck test applies to all discretionary court orders that limit freedom of expression and freedom of the press in relation to legal proceedings. Any other conclusion appears to me inconsistent with an unbroken line of authority in this Court over the past two decades. And it would tend to undermine the open court principle inextricably incorporated into the core values of s. 2(b) of the Charter. 8 The Dagenais/Mentuck test, though applicable at every stage of the judicial process, was from the outset meant to be applied in a flexible and contextual manner. A serious risk to the administration of justice at the investigative stage, for example, will often involve considerations that have become irrelevant by the time of trial. On the other hand, the perceived risk may be more difficult to demonstrate in a concrete manner at that early stage. Where a sealing order is at that stage solicited for a brief period only, this factor alone may well invite caution in opting for full and immediate disclosure. 9 Even then, however, a party seeking to limit public access to legal proceedings must rely on more than a generalized assertion that publicity could compromise investigative efficacy. If such a generalized assertion were sufficient to support a sealing order, the presumption would favour secrecy rather than openness, a plainly unacceptable result.

paragraphs.heading: Part 6. Resolving Issues And Preserving Rights

sentences.text: Notice to admit

paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 6.37 – Part 6. Resolving Issues And Preserving Rights
paragraphs.text: (1) A party may, by notice in Form 33, call on any other party to admit for the purposes of an application, originating application, streamlined trial or trial, either or both of the following: (a) any fact stated in the notice, including any fact in respect of a record; (b) any written opinion included in or attached to the notice, which must state the facts on which the opinion is based. (2) A copy of the notice must be served on each of the other parties. (3) Each of the matters for which an admission is requested is presumed to be admitted unless, within 20 days after the date of service of the notice to admit, the party to whom the notice is addressed serves on the party requesting the admission a statement that (a) denies the fact or the opinion, or both, for which an admission is requested and sets out in detail the reasons why the fact cannot be admitted or the opinion cannot be admitted, as the case requires, or (b) sets out an objection on the ground that some or all of the matters for which admissions are requested are, in whole or in part, (i) privileged, or (ii) irrelevant, improper or unnecessary. (4) A copy of the statement must be served on each of the other parties. (5) A denial by a party must fairly meet the substance of the requested admission and, when only some of the facts or opinions for which an admission is requested are denied, the denial must specify the facts or opinions that are admitted and deny only the remainder. (6) A party may amend or withdraw an admission or denial made under this rule only (a) with the Court's permission, or (b) by agreement of the parties. (7) An admission under this rule is made only for the specific purpose for which it is made and may not be used as an admission against the party making it on any other occasion, or in favour of a person other than the person requesting the admission, without the agreement of the party making the admission. (8) On application, the Court may set aside a notice to admit. Alta. Reg. 126/2023, s. 15

paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 6.37 – Part 6. Resolving Issues And Preserving Rights
paragraphs.text: Commentary § 6.37:1 Rule 6.37 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 6.37. 1. Practice Note Remember the obligation to reply to a notice to admit [R. 6.37(3)]. 2. Striking Out a Notice to Admit In Andriuk v. Merrill Lynch Canada Inc., 2011 ABQB 59, 2011 CarswellAlta 2463, 508 A.R. 114, the Defendants in an action filed pursuant to the Class Proceedings Act applied to strike out a Notice to Admit Facts “on the basis that it [was] premature, especially since pleadings [had] not closed, the issues [were] not set and the composition of any class [was] not defined”[paragraph 14]. The Defendants submitted that the “singular purpose of a Notice to Admit is directed toward proof at trial”, and relied upon the case of Canadian Southern Petroleum Ltd. v. Amoco Canada Petroleum Co. (1994), 168 A.R. 126 (Alta. Q.B.). Madam Justice Martin reviewed Canadian Southern Petroleum Ltd. v. Amoco Canada Petroleum Co., and stated, at paragraph 18, “[t]hat case cannot therefore stand for the proposition that a Notice to Admit should be set aside as premature if taken in respect of an interlocutory or pre-trial matter.” Justice Martin said, at paragraphs 20–23: [20] While such cases provide interesting historical context and some guidance, the current starting point for analysis is the new rules themselves. Under rule 1.7(1) the meaning of any rule is to be ascertained by its text, in light of the purpose and intention of the rules, and in the context in which a particular rule appears. [21] Rule 6.37(8) expressly states that a Notice to Admit can be used in “applications” as well as “originating applications, summary trial or trial”. “Application” is not a term with a defined meaning but it is used to apply to a variety of proceedings. Parties seek admissions to obviate the need to prove that fact in issue and this has value at various points in the litigation process. While a Notice to Admit may be useful, as noted in Southern Petroleum, to crystallize certain facts after discovery and before the trial begins, it is also useful at other times, including the beginning. Among the express purposes of the new rules is the intention to help parties and courts identify the real issues in dispute and to facilitate the quickest means of resolving a claim at the least expense (see rule 1.2(1)(2)). A Notice to Admit advances these purposes and is not, on its face, or by intention limited to proof of evidence at trial. [22] There will need to be a good reason, which is inconsistent with the goals and purposes of the new rules, as well as the wording and intention of rule 6.37 before a Notice to Admit will be struck: something that amounts to an abuse of process or strikes at the heart of adjudicative fairness. For example, in Ironstone v. Jansen, 2005 ABQB 21 Watson, J., as he then was, recognized in para. 20 that a Notice to Admit has a “forensic value” and its purpose is to gain a “forensic advantage”. As such he said it was not unfair to have a long Notice, when a plaintiff is asked to admit facts it ought to know, even if it involved significant work to answer. Such a Notice can only be set aside under the old 230(7) where the Notice involves a denial of adjudicative fairness. He dismissed the application to strike the Notice to Admit. In the Ontario case of Slate Falls Nation v. Canada (Attorney General) (2005), 144 A.C.W.S. 93d) 241, the equivalent to a Notice to Admit was struck by the Master as an abuse of process because there had already been significant and extensive discovery. There is nothing of this nature in the case at bar. [23] Further, Merrill created categories of objection about the type, manner and content of admissions sought including ambiguity, generality, legal determinations, conclusory statements that lack a foundation, improper form and opinions on highly specialized subjects. These objections are not such that they operate to provide grounds to set aside the Notice to Admit. A party responding to a Notice to Admit is obliged to “fairly meet the substance of the requested admission” but has a full range of response. If as matters come closer to trial it appears an earlier admission was inaccurate the rules provide that admitted facts can be withdrawn. 3. The Rule Applies to Class Proceedings Act Actions In Andriuk v. Merrill Lynch Canada Inc., 2011 ABQB 59, 2011 CarswellAlta 2463, 508 A.R. 114, Justice Martin said, at paragraphs 24-25: [24]… Does the fact that this action is taken pursuant to the C.P.A. change this conclusion? In my view it does not. The C.P.A. provides that the Rules of Court continue to apply in s.41(1). Certification is an “application” and while it is not merits based, some evidentiary foundation is required for at least four of the five statutory criteria. Hollick v. Metropolitan Toronto (Municipality), 2001 SCC 68, 2001 CarswellOnt 3577, Windsor v. Canadian Pacific Railway[2006] 8 W.W.R. 672, 60 Alta. L.R. 56. [25] Even if none of the 61 matters in the Notice to Admit are relevant to either application, which is not the case, rule 6.37 is sufficiently wide to allow a party to seek admissions to be used at trial even before a statement of defence has been filed. There is no reason why such an approach should not apply to an action filed under the C.P.A., especially since, if certification fails, the matter will proceed as an individual action. There is also no basis on which to defer the response to the Notice to Admit until after the certification application. 4. Relief Against the Deeming of Admissions The Plaintiffs in Andriuk v. Merrill Lynch Canada Inc., 2011 ABQB 59, 2011 CarswellAlta 2463, 508 A.R. 114 claimed that the Defendants, who, instead of replying to a Notice to Admit, had brought an unsuccessful application to strike out the Plaintiffs' Notice to Admit, were deemed to have admitted the facts set out in the Notice to Admit. Justice Martin concluded that such a deemed admission would be neither fair nor appropriate. At paragraphs 26-27, her Ladyship said: [26] The Plaintiffs claim that as no reply was received within the designated time that the Defendants are deemed to have admitted the facts as outlined in the Notice to Admit. The Plaintiffs assert that if Merrill now wishes to retract these deemed admissions it must meet the standards established by the Court of Appeal in Dwyer v. Fox, (1996) 181 A.R. 233, namely: that the evidence available about the fact in question is such that a determination about the truth at a trial is the only satisfactory means to settle the issue (at para. 16). [27] The nature of the relief sought by Merrill was to set aside the Notice to Admit, as contemplated under both rule 230(7) and now rule 6.37(8), which states that “on application, the Court may set aside a notice to admit.” It does not say when such an application must be taken or if, pending the hearing of the application, the running of time is suspended. On the facts of the case it would not be appropriate or fair to have the statements become deemed admissions. As early as June the Plaintiffs understood that a motion to set aside the Notice was forthcoming and it was filed on September 12, 2010. To accept the Plaintiffs' approach would only create an unnecessary step by requiring a further application to determine, which if, any deemed admissions ought to be set aside by the court. In theses circumstances Merrill is therefore given relief from the automatic application of rule 6. 37 and should be afforded an extension of time to respond. 5. The Rule Requires Service, not Filing, of the Notice [28] While the Defendant makes the point that the Notice to Admit was not filed, it was served and that is all the rules require …Andriuk v. Merrill Lynch Canada Inc. 2011 ABQB 59, per Martin, J. 6. Withdrawals of Admissions In Stringer v. Empire Life Insurance Co., 2015 ABCA 349, the Court summarized the law on withdrawal of admissions: 9 Our system of civil procedure is designed to narrow the issues to determine the true nature of the dispute: R. 1.2(2)(a). This facilitates settlement, and if settlement is not possible it shortens the eventual trial. The system encourages admissions at many stages: in the pleadings, during the questioning of adverse parties, and by more formal admissions. 10 Rule 6.37 allows any party to state facts that it believes are not truly in dispute, and to call on the other party to admit those facts. The responding party has 20 days to reply to the Notice to Admit, or to indicate, in substance, why the facts are still in dispute. If no response is received within 20 days, the facts are deemed to be admitted. Under R. 10.33(2)(b) costs can be imposed on a party that unreasonably refuses to admit facts. 11 Admissions of fact should not lightly be set aside, as that can cause prejudice to a party who has relied on those admissions, and it disrupts the natural flow of the proceedings toward settlement or trial. On the other hand, parties would be discouraged from making admissions if, once made, there could never be any retreat. A balancing of these competing objectives is required, and the Court does have the ability to permit a litigant to withdraw an admission. 12 The case law confirms that the court will consider a number of overlapping factors in deciding whether permitting withdrawal of an admission is overall in the interests of justice: (a) Was the admission intentionally made, or was it inadvertently made, or inadvertently permitted to arise by operation of the Rules; (b) What is the explanation for permitting the admission to arise, or for having made an admission which is now said to be inaccurate; (c) If there has been any delay in moving to withdraw the admission, what is the explanation for that delay; (d) Has the applicant provided sufficient evidence to demonstrate that the admitted fact may not be true, and that there is a genuine issue about an important enough fact to warrant sending the disputed fact to trial; (e) Would the withdrawal of the admission cause prejudice to the other party that cannot be remedied by costs or other terms: R. 1.5(4). None of these considerations is overriding or determinative of the issue: Hamilton v Ahmed (1999), 28 CPC (4th) 139 at para. 11 (BC Master). The relevant factors must be balanced, and, in the end, the judge or Master has a discretion whether to allow withdrawal of the admission: Goundar v Ngyuen, 2013 BCCA 251 at para. 28, 45 BCLR (5th) 68, 37 CPC (7th) 259. Where withdrawal of an admission is permitted, it will generally be done on terms as to costs or otherwise. (i) Less stringent rule In a case which dealt with an attempted withdrawal of an admission of liability in a motor vehicle accident, Hutcheon L.J.S.C. said: As I understand the authorities a judicial admission of this nature should be allowed to be withdrawn if there is no prejudice to the other party which cannot be compensated in costs, or if the court is satisfied that the admission was made inadvertently and was one that ought not to have been made. … there may be circumstances in which the defendant may not be able to show by satisfactory evidence that the fact admitted is not true, but the defendant may be able to show that an admission was made by inadvertence and that in the interest of justice the issue between the plaintiff and the defendant ought to be resolved by a trial of that issue. In my opinion the defendants in a case of this nature should not be permitted to amend their defence by withdrawing the admission of liability unless they are able to point to new facts which have come to light or to facts which were not taken into account at the time that the admission of liability was made. Such an admission is not made lightly, and it would be wrong to encourage a practice that enabled parties to admit liability one day and withdraw that admission later on the basis of a different view taken of the same facts by some other person. Oostendorp v. Sarai, [1973] 6 W.W.R. 92 at 93-94 (B.C. S.C.). (ii) More stringent rule Admissions found in pleadings of a party to an action may be withdrawn with leave of the court. Leave of the court will be granted if the party seeking to withdraw the admission establishes that the admission was made inadvertently. The party must also establish that the admission was false or, alternatively, in certain limited circumstances, that there is an issue which ought to be resolved by trial. If the court is satisfied that there will be no prejudice to the party which cannot be compensated by costs, leave to withdraw an admission should be granted. Western Mack Truck (Edmonton) Ltd. v. Heikel (1976), 1 Alta. L.R. (2d) 184 at 186 (Dist. Ct.). 7. Comment on Withdrawals In Ontario the requirement that the party seeking to withdraw the judicial admission must show that the fact admitted was not true—a requirement dating back to Canada Permanent Mortgage Corp. v. Toronto… has been modified, and in that province now the court must be satisfied only that “what is proposed to replace the admission sought to be withdrawn raises a triable issue”: see Gould v. Ariss Haulage Ltd. (1979), 27 O.R. (2d) 291 (H.C.); Antipas v. Coroneos (1988), 26 C.P.C. (2d) 63 (Ont. H.C.). The same position now applies in British Columbia. In Norlympia Seafoods Ltd. v. Dale & Co. (1982), 141 D.L.R. (3d) 733 (B.C. C.A.), at pp. 737-38, McFarlane, J.A., speaking for the court following Abacus Cities Ltd. v. Port Moody (Municipality) (1981), 26 B.C.L.R. 381 at 383 (C.A.), held that the court should allow a judicial admission to be withdrawn if, in the circumstances, the court is satisfied that it is in the interests of justice to withdraw it. The court must decide “whether or not the circumstances show that there is a triable issue which ought to be tried in the interests of justice.” In addressing that question, the factors which may be taken into consideration include whether the admission has been made inadvertently, hastily or without knowledge of the facts, or whether facts are brought to the attention of the court after the admission has been made. But McFarlane J.A., made it clear that in order to permit withdrawal of the admission it is not necessary that the party seeking leave to do so show that the admission was made by inadvertence. Nor is it necessary that the party seeking to withdraw the admission point to new facts which have come to light or to facts which were not taken into account at the time the admission was made. The sole test is whether it is shown that in the interests of justice the issue between the parties ought to be resolved by a trial of the issue. I must say that, if the circumstances in which permission may be granted to allow a judicial admission to be withdrawn and were the issue now before me, I would be inclined to adopt the position now accepted in Ontario and British Columbia. Davies v. Edmonton (City) (1991), 84 Alta. L.R. (2d) 121 (Q.B.), at 125-26, per McDonald J. The above comments deal with withdrawal of admissions specifically made. With respect to deemed admissions, McDonald J. continued: … That being so, [i.e., adopting the position now accepted in Ontario and British Columbia] it would be inconsistent to adopt a more rigorous test for allowing withdrawal of a deemed admission—one that is deemed to have occurred by virtue of the failure to respond to a notice to admit facts. The deemed admission in this case has occurred not as a result of a conscious and deliberate decision to allow the rule to have the effect of deeming an admission to have been made. Rather, the rule has been triggered by an inadvertent failure to respond. In such circumstances I consider that it would be unjust not to allow extension of the time for responding, so long as the material filed shows that there is a triable issue which ought to be tried in the interests of justice. Subordinate to that overriding test are considerations such as whether withdrawal of the admission would prejudice the other party, or whether any prejudice that would result can be compensated in costs. That consideration is relevant to “the interests of justice.” This position reflects the following annotation of R. 36(b) of the United States Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (West Publishing) which, like our rule, allows the court to permit withdrawal (or amendment) of an admission deemed to have been admitted in the absence of service of a written objection to a request for the admission of the truth of a matter: This provision emphasizes the importance of having the action resolved on the merits, while at the same time assuring each party that justified reliance on an admission in preparation for trial will not operate to his prejudice. In Canada (Attorney General) v. Harrison (February 28, 1985) (unreported), Master Funduk, said that the principles applicable to the withdrawal of admissions in pleadings “are equally applicable to the deemed admissions created by R. 230.” He added: “There is no logical basis for treating an admission differently.” With respect, I do not agree. If there is to be a more rigorous test for the withdrawal of judicial admission (which I do not think should be so), the reason for difference would lie in the distinction between a conscious, advertent admission and an inadvertent admission. If a party has consciously admitted a fact, he has presumably had good reason in fact for doing so, and the court should (perhaps) be more reluctant to allow withdrawal of such an admission than in the case of a deemed admission resulting from inadvertence. Davies v. Edmonton (City), supra, at 126. The Court of Appeal, with some reservation, has adopted the reasoning of McDonald J.: This case requires this court to state a rule about what Queen's Bench should do when counsel fails to respond to a Notice to Admit. Rule 230(5) permits a judge to allow a party to withdraw a deemed admission “on such terms as may be just”. It is the proper exercise of this power that is engaged here. . . . . . Counsel for the appellant defendant suggested we adopt the approach taken by the British Columbia Court of Appeal in Norlympia Seafoods Ltd. et al. v. Dale & Co. (1982), 41 B.C.L.R. 145 (C.A.). He argued that in every case the decision should turn not so much on the behaviour of counsel as on the cogency of the evidence about the fact admitted. Counsel for the respondent plaintiff replied that permission to withdraw a deemed admission should be limited to cases where the cause of the admission is mere haste or inadvertence, not gross neglect or conscious decision. Norlympia was a case about an admission in a pleading. There was no suggestion that it was made merely by reason of haste or inadvertence, but the chambers judge nevertheless permitted the party to withdraw it. He did so because the material before him satisfied him that the truth of the matter was at variance with the admission. Citing the rule in Abacus Cities Ltd. v. Port Moody (Municipality) (1981), 26 B.C.L.R. 381 (C.A.), that a court should permit a party to withdraw a judicial admission if to do so is in the interests of justice, which is merely a restatement of the rule, the Court of Appeal affirmed. McFarlane, J.A., seemed to suggest that the interests of justice require withdrawal in any case where the issue of fact is “triable”, by which we think he meant that the evidence on the point is not straightforward, and an issue of credibility or reasonable inference, or something like that, has arisen. He did concede that the behaviour of counsel may be of help in determining this point. We take it he meant by this that a careful, considered, and conscious decision to admit is strong evidence to justify an inference that an issue is not triable. This approach has been accepted in Queen's Bench. See Davies et al. v. Edmonton (City) and Baker (1991), 84 Alta. L.R. (2d) 121 (Q.B.). McDonald, J. (as he then was), there noted that the earlier Ontario practice had been to demand of the persons who would withdraw an admission that they show that the admission was not the truth, but that now the Ontario practice required only that a triable issue be shown. He also noted that cases about admissions in pleadings sometimes involve conscious decisions to admit, as seems to have been the case in Norlympia. Even in those cases, the admitters are permitted to withdraw the admission if they can show a triable issue about the fact in question. It is difficult to see, McDonald, J., rightly observed, how one can make a sterner rule for deemed admissions if that is the rule for explicit admissions. Counsel for the respondent defendant replies that the rule about withdrawal should apply only in the case of inadvertent admissions, and not where there has been a conscious decision or gross neglect. To be sure, there are many cases where it is said that the making of the admission must be inadvertent. That is easy to say when the admission before the court was inadvertently made. Only a few cases deal with a situation where the admission was accounted for by something other than inadvertence. And most of them permit withdrawal if the admitted fact is untrue or there is a serious question whether it is true. See, for example, Antipas v. Coroneos (1988), 26 C.P.C. (2d) 63 (Ont. H.C.). The important Canadian cases are all summarized in the Stevenson & Côté, Civil Procedure Guide, Edmonton, Alberta: Juriliber, 1996, at pp. 994-996. . . . . . Admissions are a key part of normal and efficient litigation, whether made in pleadings, at Examinations, or by other means, including the deemed admission in response to a Notice to Admit. The adversary system would not work if counsel could lightly resile from an admission. To some, that sound view would justify an absolute, or near-absolute, rule against withdrawal. In many contexts, however, courts have stepped back from a rule so harsh as that. It is quite correct that every exception complicates litigation. It is also true that there is more to swift justice than just swiftness. We must strike the right balance between efficiency and fairness. As has been observed in the Civil Procedure Guide, p. 600, the harsher rule, which would demand that there be no exceptions except for inadvertent admissions or for an admission proven to be false, may discourage counsel from ever making admissions. With some reservations, we agree with and adopt the approach taken by McDonald, J. Even if the admission was one consciously and deliberately made, a judge should permit withdrawal in any case where the person who made an admission, whether explicit or deemed, has demonstrated to the satisfaction of the judge that the evidence available about the fact in question is such that a determination of the truth at a trial is the only satisfactory means to settle the issue. In other words, the pursuit of truth should take priority over the discipline of imprudence. The first reservation is that pursuit of truth can also go off the track because of a lack of discipline in the trial or pretrial process. We would therefore add the condition, perhaps implicit in earlier Alberta cases, that the person who would withdraw an admission must also show that withdrawal would not cause a substantial prejudice to the party opposite that could not be compensated for by costs. The second reservation is about our apprehension that the rule stated by McDonald, J., may be seen by counsel as an invitation not to deal seriously and promptly with case management tools like the Notice to Admit. One could argue that the rule could totally undermine one purpose of the Notice. That surely is to require the side opposite to assess its case promptly, within the time provided in the Rules, and thus spare the server of the notice the need to prepare for trial on the stated facts. If the deemed admission can be nullified after the other side finally gets around to making inquiries, the goal of early resolution is utterly lost. Counsel who receive the Notice may reason thus: I shall do nothing. If later I decide the fact is not disputable, no harm done. On the other hand, if later I decide I can challenge it, all I need to do is show my newly found evidence to the judge, and I shall be relieved of the admission. Either way, I can safely prepare at the pace I choose and ignore this Notice. And counsel who consider whether to serve a notice may well decide, because of all this, not to bother. Whatever the reason, the procedure is underused. Perhaps this is why. The solution is that, in every case where the failure to deny is not merely inadvertent, the party must be subject to a substantial and exemplary penalty. Even when the error is inadvertent, the other side should have thrown-away costs. When it is more serious, the penalty must bite, and bite hard. As to terms, we are well-guided by what this court earlier said about indulgences granted to parties who have delayed suits: The court should be flexible and imaginative in devising such terms. Suitable terms include payment forthwith of heavy (and) truly compensatory costs or other indemnities, e.g. for extra trial expenses … The court may craft terms which will weaken or strengthen the means used at trial to prove certain disputed facts, modifying the ordinary rules of evidence accordingly … The court may even require that certain facts be admitted before trial, or that certain claims be modified or capped … The appellant plaintiff seeks an indulgence, and to get it he must be prepared to swallow a stiff dose of rough justice and practical medicine. (Hummell v. St. Mary's River Irrigation District (1992), 131 A.R. 104 (C.A.)) We emphasize that the failure here that generated the need for a penalty was the failure to respond promptly to a lawful Notice. We do not propose to punish the party for failing to admit a fact. That sort of issue does not arise in this case. Nor does the reasonableness of the Notice, or any of its parts. A party served with a Notice has other choices, beyond either an admission or a denial, and that is either to move to strike a Notice as unreasonable in the sense of making an unreasonable demand or to request an extension of time. The question of the reasonableness or timeliness of the Notice was not put in issue here. The third reservation is that, where the decision to admit is conscious and deliberate and without reasonable excuse, that decision must count for something. A judge should not lightly say that an issue is triable when counsel came to a different conclusion. Indeed, without more, we think a judge may safely infer that such a decision decides the triability issue. The fourth reservation is about any attempt to extend this rule to the attempted withdrawal of an admission on appeal. While that is not the issue before us, we do emphasize that there are different considerations on appeal. The entire purpose of a trial is to settle matters of fact once and for all. Hoysted v. Commissioner of Taxation, [1926] A.C. 155. Dwyer v. Fox (1996), 181 A.R. 223 (C.A.), at 225-29, per Kerans J.A. The test in Davies v. Edmonton (City) (1991), 84 Alta. L.R. (2d) 121 (Q.B.) was summarized by Master Funduk in Kaboni v. Domes (1994), 150 A.R. 161 (Q.B.), at p. 164 where the learned Master said: The defendant must show that (a) the failure to serve a reply was not done deliberately, and (b) “the material filed shows that there is a triable issue which ought to be tried in the interests of justice”. Master Funduk in Kaboni then went on to discuss the second part of the test (i.e., the material that must show a triable issue). He said at p. 164: It is not sufficient for the reply itself to meet the second part of the test. That would reduce the second part of the test to one of draftsmanship. In a case such as this there must be some evidence to raise an arguable issue about the admitted facts. The defendant does not have to establish that the admitted facts are not true, merely that there is an arguable issue about those facts. See also the annotation “Admissions” under R. 130, supra, and “Withdrawal of Informal Admission” under R. 162, supra. 8. Objections In MacKenzie v. Estate of Michael Gregory, 2022 ABQB 521, 2022 CarswellAlta 2047, Justice Hollins had before her this question: if a party objects to making an admission which is sought, must that party provide grounds for the objection? Her Ladyship said: [26] … Rule 6.37(2)(b)(ii) can only fulfil its objective if the basis for the objection—which is wholly within the knowledge of the responding party - is disclosed. Without it, there is no discernible purpose or intention to the Rule; Rule 1.7(1). [27] In my view, an objection to an admission sought must: (1) delineate whether the objection is because the admission sought is irrelevant, improper or unnecessary; and (2) offer a basic reason for why that is so, in the view of the responding party. Many of the possibilities have been seen in other cases. For example, in Andriuk, the following bases for objections were identified: ambiguity, generality, legal determinations, conclusory statements that lack a foundation, improper form and opinions on highly specialized subjects. In Canada Southern Petroleum Ltd v Amoco Canada Petroleum Co, 1994 CarswellAlta 716 O’Leary, J (as he then was) also listed a number of possible responses that could be proper objections e.g. lack of independent knowledge, requiring the interpretation of a document or a legal conclusion, a document that speaks for itself or a request that is too vague to answer; paras.10-14. Her Ladyship’s reference to “Rule 6.37(2)(b)(ii)” would seem to be an inadvertent error. The Rule referred to is Rule 6.37(3)((b)(ii). 9. Costs The plaintiff asks for additional costs because the defendant failed to admit two facts when given the opportunity to do so in answer to a notice to admit. The notice to admit process is provided in the Rules in an effort to shorten trials and thereby make them less costly. When a litigant wrongly fails to admit a fact which it has been requested to admit, and where the originating party is then put to the trouble and expense of calling evidence to prove the fact in issue, the originating party is entitled to costs in relation to that evidence. Where the originating party is also the successful party, that party is entitled to additional costs to reflect the time and trouble of calling the disputed evidence, even though the originating party will get costs that include all the time taken for the trial. This is because the tariff only compensates the successful party for a portion of the costs expended on the trial. Additional compensation can, and should, be awarded where appropriate. Waterous Investments Inc. v. Liberton Holdings Ltd. (1996), 183 A.R. 229 (Q.B.), at 235, per Veit J. In Ellis v. Friedland (2000), 276 A.R. 364 (Q.B.), the defendant, having been successful at trial, sought “increased costs because the plaintiff did not admit substantial and material facts as stated in the defendant's Notices to Admit, and such facts were later proven at trial.” In other words, the defendant was seeking costs in excess of those incurred in proving the fact which should have been admitted. McMahon J. considered Rule 230(4), and, in denying the application for additional costs, said, at p. 367: It is clear that the penalty for an unreasonable refusal to admit facts is payment of costs for proving that matter. There is no provision in R. 230(4) for increasing a costs award. In Patterson v. Hryciuk, 2005 ABQB 136, 2005 CarswellAlta 309, 45 Alta. L.R. (4th) 240, at pp. 250-251, Macklin J. said the following concerning the award of costs for facts not admitted after service of a Notice to Admit: The service of a Notice to Admit Facts is not a procedure to be invoked by a party in an attempt to increase its potential costs award in the same manner as the compromise procedures set out in Part 12 of the Rules. The purpose of a Notice to Admit Facts is to try and expedite the trial procedure and minimize or reduce costs by obviating the necessity of calling certain evidence. Where the evidence necessary to be called is going to be called in any event and the requested admissions can be given in evidence with minimal or no additional time or expense involved, it is inappropriate to try and use the rule to invoke cost penalties in an attempt to increase the potential costs award following trial. 10. Rule Applies to Civil Judicial Review Applications It is the conclusion of this Court that the procedure stipulated in Rule 230 is available to the Applicant in the present civil judicial review application. Consideration by the Court of the applicability of any of the general rules to a judicial review procedure must first begin with a consideration of those rules themselves. Rule 753.19 specifically directs the applicability of all general rules to judicial review matters unless otherwise “provided specificially in that part.” There is no special provision excluding Rule 230 in Part 56.1. When considering the application of any interlocutory procedural rule to judicial review applications, the Court is also entitled to consider the objectives behind the implementation of the new judicial review procedures… In principle, technical objections to the applicablility of the general rules are to be discouraged… In the Alberta Rules, the use of the Notice relates to any “cause, matter or issue”. A proceeding for judicial review is to be commenced by Originating Notice in Alberta. By definition that is a document by which an action is initiated. Surely there can be no meaningful distinction between [an]“action” and “cause, matter or issue.” . . . . . There appears to this Court no apparent practical reason for excluding the use of this procedure in such a case as this. There may be some situations of judicial review in which Rule 230 ought not to be available. Certainly, the scope for its use where the judicial review is based on alleged error within the jurisdiction of a lower tribunal or officer on the face of the record would appear to be limited. Alberta River Conservation Foundation v. Alberta (Minister of Environmental Protection) (1998), 58 Alta. L.R. (3d) 287 (Q.B.), at 292-94, per Wilkins J.

Striking Out a Notice to Admit In Andriuk v.
Merrill Lynch Canada Inc., 2011 ABQB 59, 2011 CarswellAlta 2463, 508 A.R.

114, the Defendants in an action filed pursuant to the Class Proceedings Act applied to strike out a Notice to Admit Facts “on the basis that it [was] premature, especially since pleadings [had] not closed, the issues [were] not set and the composition of any class [was] not defined”[paragraph 14].
The Defendants submitted that the “singular purpose of a Notice to Admit is directed toward proof at trial”, and relied upon the case of Canadian Southern Petroleum Ltd. v.
Amoco Canada Petroleum Co.
126 (Alta.
Madam Justice Martin reviewed Canadian Southern Petroleum Ltd. v.

Amoco Canada Petroleum Co., and stated, at paragraph 18, “[t]hat case cannot therefore stand for the proposition that a Notice to Admit should be set aside as premature if taken in respect of an interlocutory or pre-trial matter.” Justice Martin said, at paragraphs 20–23: [20] While such cases provide interesting historical context and some guidance, the current starting point for analysis is the new rules themselves.
Under rule 1.7(1) the meaning of any rule is to be ascertained by its text, in light of the purpose and intention of the rules, and in the context in which a particular rule appears.

[21] Rule 6.37(8) expressly states that a Notice to Admit can be used in “applications” as well as “originating applications, summary trial or trial”. “Application” is not a term with a defined meaning but it is used to apply to a variety of proceedings.
Parties seek admissions to obviate the need to prove that fact in issue and this has value at various points in the litigation process.

While a Notice to Admit may be useful, as noted in Southern Petroleum, to crystallize certain facts after discovery and before the trial begins, it is also useful at other times, including the beginning.

Among the express purposes of the new rules is the intention to help parties and courts identify the real issues in dispute and to facilitate the quickest means of resolving a claim at the least expense (see rule 1.2(1)(2)).
A Notice to Admit advances these purposes and is not, on its face, or by intention limited to proof of evidence at trial.

[22] There will need to be a good reason, which is inconsistent with the goals and purposes of the new rules, as well as the wording and intention of rule 6.37 before a Notice to Admit will be struck: something that amounts to an abuse of process or strikes at the heart of adjudicative fairness.
For example, in Ironstone v.
Jansen, 2005 ABQB 21 Watson, J., as he then was, recognized in para.
20 that a Notice to Admit has a “forensic value” and its purpose is to gain a “forensic advantage”.
As such he said it was not unfair to have a long Notice, when a plaintiff is asked to admit facts it ought to know, even if it involved significant work to answer.
Such a Notice can only be set aside under the old 230(7) where the Notice involves a denial of adjudicative fairness.
He dismissed the application to strike the Notice to Admit.
In the Ontario case of Slate Falls Nation v.
Canada (Attorney General) (2005), 144 A.C.W.S.
93d) 241, the equivalent to a Notice to Admit was struck by the Master as an abuse of process because there had already been significant and extensive discovery.
There is nothing of this nature in the case at bar.

[23] Further, Merrill created categories of objection about the type, manner and content of admissions sought including ambiguity, generality, legal determinations, conclusory statements that lack a foundation, improper form and opinions on highly specialized subjects.
These objections are not such that they operate to provide grounds to set aside the Notice to Admit.
A party responding to a Notice to Admit is obliged to “fairly meet the substance of the requested admission” but has a full range of response.
If as matters come closer to trial it appears an earlier admission was inaccurate the rules provide that admitted facts can be withdrawn.
The Rule Applies to Class Proceedings Act Actions In Andriuk v.
Merrill Lynch Canada Inc., 2011 ABQB 59, 2011 CarswellAlta 2463, 508 A.R.
114, Justice Martin said, at paragraphs 24-25: [24]… Does the fact that this action is taken pursuant to the C.P.A. change this conclusion?
In my view it does not.
The C.P.A. provides that the Rules of Court continue to apply in s.41(1).
Certification is an “application” and while it is not merits based, some evidentiary foundation is required for at least four of the five statutory criteria.
Hollick v.
Metropolitan Toronto (Municipality), 2001 SCC 68, 2001 CarswellOnt 3577, Windsor v.
Canadian Pacific Railway[2006] 8 W.W.R.
L.R.

[25] Even if none of the 61 matters in the Notice to Admit are relevant to either application, which is not the case, rule 6.37 is sufficiently wide to allow a party to seek admissions to be used at trial even before a statement of defence has been filed.
There is no reason why such an approach should not apply to an action filed under the C.P.A., especially since, if certification fails, the matter will proceed as an individual action.
There is also no basis on which to defer the response to the Notice to Admit until after the certification application.
Relief Against the Deeming of Admissions The Plaintiffs in Andriuk v.
Merrill Lynch Canada Inc., 2011 ABQB 59, 2011 CarswellAlta 2463, 508 A.R.

114 claimed that the Defendants, who, instead of replying to a Notice to Admit, had brought an unsuccessful application to strike out the Plaintiffs' Notice to Admit, were deemed to have admitted the facts set out in the Notice to Admit.
Justice Martin concluded that such a deemed admission would be neither fair nor appropriate.

At paragraphs 26-27, her Ladyship said: [26] The Plaintiffs claim that as no reply was received within the designated time that the Defendants are deemed to have admitted the facts as outlined in the Notice to Admit.
The Plaintiffs assert that if Merrill now wishes to retract these deemed admissions it must meet the standards established by the Court of Appeal in Dwyer v.
233, namely: that the evidence available about the fact in question is such that a determination about the truth at a trial is the only satisfactory means to settle the issue (at para.

[27] The nature of the relief sought by Merrill was to set aside the Notice to Admit, as contemplated under both rule 230(7) and now rule 6.37(8), which states that “on application, the Court may set aside a notice to admit.” It does not say when such an application must be taken or if, pending the hearing of the application, the running of time is suspended.
On the facts of the case it would not be appropriate or fair to have the statements become deemed admissions.
As early as June the Plaintiffs understood that a motion to set aside the Notice was forthcoming and it was filed on September 12, 2010.
To accept the Plaintiffs' approach would only create an unnecessary step by requiring a further application to determine, which if, any deemed admissions ought to be set aside by the court.
In theses circumstances Merrill is therefore given relief from the automatic application of rule 6.
37 and should be afforded an extension of time to respond.
The Rule Requires Service, not Filing, of the Notice [28] While the Defendant makes the point that the Notice to Admit was not filed, it was served and that is all the rules require …Andriuk v.
Merrill Lynch Canada Inc.
2011 ABQB 59, per Martin, J.
Withdrawals of Admissions In Stringer v.

Empire Life Insurance Co., 2015 ABCA 349, the Court summarized the law on withdrawal of admissions: 9 Our system of civil procedure is designed to narrow the issues to determine the true nature of the dispute: R.
This facilitates settlement, and if settlement is not possible it shortens the eventual trial.
The system encourages admissions at many stages: in the pleadings, during the questioning of adverse parties, and by more formal admissions.
10 Rule 6.37 allows any party to state facts that it believes are not truly in dispute, and to call on the other party to admit those facts.
The responding party has 20 days to reply to the Notice to Admit, or to indicate, in substance, why the facts are still in dispute.
If no response is received within 20 days, the facts are deemed to be admitted.
Under R.
10.33(2)(b) costs can be imposed on a party that unreasonably refuses to admit facts.

11 Admissions of fact should not lightly be set aside, as that can cause prejudice to a party who has relied on those admissions, and it disrupts the natural flow of the proceedings toward settlement or trial.
On the other hand, parties would be discouraged from making admissions if, once made, there could never be any retreat.
A balancing of these competing objectives is required, and the Court does have the ability to permit a litigant to withdraw an admission.
12 The case law confirms that the court will consider a number of overlapping factors in deciding whether permitting withdrawal of an admission is overall in the interests of justice:
(a) Was the admission intentionally made, or was it inadvertently made, or inadvertently permitted to arise by operation of the Rules
(b) What is the explanation for permitting the admission to arise, or for having made an admission which is now said to be inaccurate
(c) If there has been any delay in moving to withdraw the admission, what is the explanation for that delay

(d) Has the applicant provided sufficient evidence to demonstrate that the admitted fact may not be true, and that there is a genuine issue about an important enough fact to warrant sending the disputed fact to trial
(e) Would the withdrawal of the admission cause prejudice to the other party that cannot be remedied by costs or other terms: R.
None of these considerations is overriding or determinative of the issue: Hamilton v Ahmed (1999), 28 CPC (4th) 139 at para.
11 (BC Master).
The relevant factors must be balanced, and, in the end, the judge or Master has a discretion whether to allow withdrawal of the admission: Goundar v Ngyuen, 2013 BCCA 251 at para.
Where withdrawal of an admission is permitted, it will generally be done on terms as to costs or otherwise.

(i) Less stringent rule In a case which dealt with an attempted withdrawal of an admission of liability in a motor vehicle accident, Hutcheon L.J.S.C. said: As I understand the authorities a judicial admission of this nature should be allowed to be withdrawn if there is no prejudice to the other party which cannot be compensated in costs, or if the court is satisfied that the admission was made inadvertently and was one that ought not to have been made. … there may be circumstances in which the defendant may not be able to show by satisfactory evidence that the fact admitted is not true, but the defendant may be able to show that an admission was made by inadvertence and that in the interest of justice the issue between the plaintiff and the defendant ought to be resolved by a trial of that issue.

In my opinion the defendants in a case of this nature should not be permitted to amend their defence by withdrawing the admission of liability unless they are able to point to new facts which have come to light or to facts which were not taken into account at the time that the admission of liability was made.

Such an admission is not made lightly, and it would be wrong to encourage a practice that enabled parties to admit liability one day and withdraw that admission later on the basis of a different view taken of the same facts by some other person.
Oostendorp v.
Sarai, [1973] 6 W.W.R.
(ii) More stringent rule Admissions found in pleadings of a party to an action may be withdrawn with leave of the court.
Leave of the court will be granted if the party seeking to withdraw the admission establishes that the admission was made inadvertently.
The party must also establish that the admission was false or, alternatively, in certain limited circumstances, that there is an issue which ought to be resolved by trial.
If the court is satisfied that there will be no prejudice to the party which cannot be compensated by costs, leave to withdraw an admission should be granted.
Western Mack Truck (Edmonton) Ltd. v.
Heikel (1976), 1 Alta.
L.R.
Ct.).

Comment on Withdrawals In Ontario the requirement that the party seeking to withdraw the judicial admission must show that the fact admitted was not true—a requirement dating back to Canada Permanent Mortgage Corp. v.
Toronto… has been modified, and in that province now the court must be satisfied only that “what is proposed to replace the admission sought to be withdrawn raises a triable issue”: see Gould v.
Ariss Haulage Ltd.
(2d) 291 (H.C.); Antipas v.
Coroneos (1988), 26 C.P.C.
The same position now applies in British Columbia.
In Norlympia Seafoods Ltd. v.
Dale & Co.
C.A.), at pp.
737-38, McFarlane, J.A., speaking for the court following Abacus Cities Ltd. v.
Port Moody (Municipality) (1981), 26 B.C.L.R.
381 at 383 (C.A.), held that the court should allow a judicial admission to be withdrawn if, in the circumstances, the court is satisfied that it is in the interests of justice to withdraw it.

The court must decide “whether or not the circumstances show that there is a triable issue which ought to be tried in the interests of justice.” In addressing that question, the factors which may be taken into consideration include whether the admission has been made inadvertently, hastily or without knowledge of the facts, or whether facts are brought to the attention of the court after the admission has been made.
But McFarlane J.A., made it clear that in order to permit withdrawal of the admission it is not necessary that the party seeking leave to do so show that the admission was made by inadvertence.
Nor is it necessary that the party seeking to withdraw the admission point to new facts which have come to light or to facts which were not taken into account at the time the admission was made.
The sole test is whether it is shown that in the interests of justice the issue between the parties ought to be resolved by a trial of the issue.

I must say that, if the circumstances in which permission may be granted to allow a judicial admission to be withdrawn and were the issue now before me, I would be inclined to adopt the position now accepted in Ontario and British Columbia.
Davies v.
Edmonton (City) (1991), 84 Alta.
L.R.
(2d) 121 (Q.B.), at 125-26, per McDonald J.
The above comments deal with withdrawal of admissions specifically made.

With respect to deemed admissions, McDonald J. continued: … That being so, [i.e., adopting the position now accepted in Ontario and British Columbia] it would be inconsistent to adopt a more rigorous test for allowing withdrawal of a deemed admission—one that is deemed to have occurred by virtue of the failure to respond to a notice to admit facts.
The deemed admission in this case has occurred not as a result of a conscious and deliberate decision to allow the rule to have the effect of deeming an admission to have been made.
Rather, the rule has been triggered by an inadvertent failure to respond.

In such circumstances I consider that it would be unjust not to allow extension of the time for responding, so long as the material filed shows that there is a triable issue which ought to be tried in the interests of justice.

Subordinate to that overriding test are considerations such as whether withdrawal of the admission would prejudice the other party, or whether any prejudice that would result can be compensated in costs.
That consideration is relevant to “the interests of justice.” This position reflects the following annotation of R.

36(b) of the United States Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (West Publishing) which, like our rule, allows the court to permit withdrawal (or amendment) of an admission deemed to have been admitted in the absence of service of a written objection to a request for the admission of the truth of a matter: This provision emphasizes the importance of having the action resolved on the merits, while at the same time assuring each party that justified reliance on an admission in preparation for trial will not operate to his prejudice.
In Canada (Attorney General) v.

Harrison (February 28, 1985) (unreported), Master Funduk, said that the principles applicable to the withdrawal of admissions in pleadings “are equally applicable to the deemed admissions created by R.
230.” He added: “There is no logical basis for treating an admission differently.” With respect, I do not agree.

If there is to be a more rigorous test for the withdrawal of judicial admission (which I do not think should be so), the reason for difference would lie in the distinction between a conscious, advertent admission and an inadvertent admission.
If a party has consciously admitted a fact, he has presumably had good reason in fact for doing so, and the court should
(perhaps) be more reluctant to allow withdrawal of such an admission than in the case of a deemed admission resulting from inadvertence.
Davies v.
Edmonton (City), supra, at 126.

The Court of Appeal, with some reservation, has adopted the reasoning of McDonald J.: This case requires this court to state a rule about what Queen's Bench should do when counsel fails to respond to a Notice to Admit.
Rule 230(5) permits a judge to allow a party to withdraw a deemed admission “on such terms as may be just”.
It is the proper exercise of this power that is engaged here. . . . . .
Counsel for the appellant defendant suggested we adopt the approach taken by the British Columbia Court of Appeal in Norlympia Seafoods Ltd. et al. v.
Dale & Co.
He argued that in every case the decision should turn not so much on the behaviour of counsel as on the cogency of the evidence about the fact admitted.

Counsel for the respondent plaintiff replied that permission to withdraw a deemed admission should be limited to cases where the cause of the admission is mere haste or inadvertence, not gross neglect or conscious decision.
Norlympia was a case about an admission in a pleading.
There was no suggestion that it was made merely by reason of haste or inadvertence, but the chambers judge nevertheless permitted the party to withdraw it.
He did so because the material before him satisfied him that the truth of the matter was at variance with the admission.
Citing the rule in Abacus Cities Ltd. v.
Port Moody (Municipality) (1981), 26 B.C.L.R.
381 (C.A.), that a court should permit a party to withdraw a judicial admission if to do so is in the interests of justice, which is merely a restatement of the rule, the Court of Appeal affirmed.

McFarlane, J.A., seemed to suggest that the interests of justice require withdrawal in any case where the issue of fact is “triable”, by which we think he meant that the evidence on the point is not straightforward, and an issue of credibility or reasonable inference, or something like that, has arisen.
He did concede that the behaviour of counsel may be of help in determining this point.
We take it he meant by this that a careful, considered, and conscious decision to admit is strong evidence to justify an inference that an issue is not triable.
This approach has been accepted in Queen's Bench.
See Davies et al. v.
Edmonton (City) and Baker (1991), 84 Alta.
L.R.
McDonald, J.

(as he then was), there noted that the earlier Ontario practice had been to demand of the persons who would withdraw an admission that they show that the admission was not the truth, but that now the Ontario practice required only that a triable issue be shown.
He also noted that cases about admissions in pleadings sometimes involve conscious decisions to admit, as seems to have been the case in Norlympia.
Even in those cases, the admitters are permitted to withdraw the admission if they can show a triable issue about the fact in question.
It is difficult to see, McDonald, J., rightly observed, how one can make a sterner rule for deemed admissions if that is the rule for explicit admissions.

Counsel for the respondent defendant replies that the rule about withdrawal should apply only in the case of inadvertent admissions, and not where there has been a conscious decision or gross neglect.
To be sure, there are many cases where it is said that the making of the admission must be inadvertent.
That is easy to say when the admission before the court was inadvertently made.
Only a few cases deal with a situation where the admission was accounted for by something other than inadvertence.
And most of them permit withdrawal if the admitted fact is untrue or there is a serious question whether it is true.
See, for example, Antipas v.
Coroneos (1988), 26 C.P.C.
The important Canadian cases are all summarized in the Stevenson & Côté, Civil Procedure Guide, Edmonton, Alberta: Juriliber, 1996, at pp.
Admissions are a key part of normal and efficient litigation, whether made in pleadings, at Examinations, or by other means, including the deemed admission in response to a Notice to Admit.
The adversary system would not work if counsel could lightly resile from an admission.
To some, that sound view would justify an absolute, or near-absolute, rule against withdrawal.
In many contexts, however, courts have stepped back from a rule so harsh as that.
It is quite correct that every exception complicates litigation.
It is also true that there is more to swift justice than just swiftness.
We must strike the right balance between efficiency and fairness.
As has been observed in the Civil Procedure Guide, p.
600, the harsher rule, which would demand that there be no exceptions except for inadvertent admissions or for an admission proven to be false, may discourage counsel from ever making admissions.
With some reservations, we agree with and adopt the approach taken by McDonald, J.

Even if the admission was one consciously and deliberately made, a judge should permit withdrawal in any case where the person who made an admission, whether explicit or deemed, has demonstrated to the satisfaction of the judge that the evidence available about the fact in question is such that a determination of the truth at a trial is the only satisfactory means to settle the issue.
In other words, the pursuit of truth should take priority over the discipline of imprudence.
The first reservation is that pursuit of truth can also go off the track because of a lack of discipline in the trial or pretrial process.

We would therefore add the condition, perhaps implicit in earlier Alberta cases, that the person who would withdraw an admission must also show that withdrawal would not cause a substantial prejudice to the party opposite that could not be compensated for by costs.

The second reservation is about our apprehension that the rule stated by McDonald, J., may be seen by counsel as an invitation not to deal seriously and promptly with case management tools like the Notice to Admit.
One could argue that the rule could totally undermine one purpose of the Notice.

That surely is to require the side opposite to assess its case promptly, within the time provided in the Rules, and thus spare the server of the notice the need to prepare for trial on the stated facts.
If the deemed admission can be nullified after the other side finally gets around to making inquiries, the goal of early resolution is utterly lost.
Counsel who receive the Notice may reason thus: I shall do nothing.
If later I decide the fact is not disputable, no harm done.
On the other hand, if later I decide I can challenge it, all I need to do is show my newly found evidence to the judge, and I shall be relieved of the admission.
Either way, I can safely prepare at the pace I choose and ignore this Notice.
And counsel who consider whether to serve a notice may well decide, because of all this, not to bother.
Whatever the reason, the procedure is underused.
Perhaps this is why.
The solution is that, in every case where the failure to deny is not merely inadvertent, the party must be subject to a substantial and exemplary penalty.
Even when the error is inadvertent, the other side should have thrown-away costs.
When it is more serious, the penalty must bite, and bite hard.
As to terms, we are well-guided by what this court earlier said about indulgences granted to parties who have delayed suits: The court should be flexible and imaginative in devising such terms.
Suitable terms include payment forthwith of heavy

(and) truly compensatory costs or other indemnities, e.g. for extra trial expenses … The court may craft terms which will weaken or strengthen the means used at trial to prove certain disputed facts, modifying the ordinary rules of evidence accordingly … The court may even require that certain facts be admitted before trial, or that certain claims be modified or capped … The appellant plaintiff seeks an indulgence, and to get it he must be prepared to swallow a stiff dose of rough justice and practical medicine.
(Hummell v.
St.
Mary's River Irrigation District (1992), 131 A.R.
104 (C.A.)) We emphasize that the failure here that generated the need for a penalty was the failure to respond promptly to a lawful Notice.
We do not propose to punish the party for failing to admit a fact.
That sort of issue does not arise in this case.
Nor does the reasonableness of the Notice, or any of its parts.

A party served with a Notice has other choices, beyond either an admission or a denial, and that is either to move to strike a Notice as unreasonable in the sense of making an unreasonable demand or to request an extension of time.
The question of the reasonableness or timeliness of the Notice was not put in issue here.
The third reservation is that, where the decision to admit is conscious and deliberate and without reasonable excuse, that decision must count for something.
A judge should not lightly say that an issue is triable when counsel came to a different conclusion.
Indeed, without more, we think a judge may safely infer that such a decision decides the triability issue.
The fourth reservation is about any attempt to extend this rule to the attempted withdrawal of an admission on appeal.
While that is not the issue before us, we do emphasize that there are different considerations on appeal.
The entire purpose of a trial is to settle matters of fact once and for all.
Hoysted v.
Commissioner of Taxation, [1926] A.C.
Dwyer v.
223 (C.A.), at 225-29, per Kerans J.A.
The test in Davies v.
Edmonton (City) (1991), 84 Alta.
L.R.
(2d) 121 (Q.B.) was summarized by Master Funduk in Kaboni v.
164 where the learned Master said: The defendant must show that
(a) the failure to serve a reply was not done deliberately, and
(b) “the material filed shows that there is a triable issue which ought to be tried in the interests of justice”.
Master Funduk in Kaboni then went on to discuss the second part of the test (i.e., the material that must show a triable issue).
He said at p.
164: It is not sufficient for the reply itself to meet the second part of the test.
That would reduce the second part of the test to one of draftsmanship.
In a case such as this there must be some evidence to raise an arguable issue about the admitted facts.
The defendant does not have to establish that the admitted facts are not true, merely that there is an arguable issue about those facts.
See also the annotation “Admissions” under R.
130, supra, and “Withdrawal of Informal Admission” under R.
162, supra.
Objections In MacKenzie v.

Estate of Michael Gregory, 2022 ABQB 521, 2022 CarswellAlta 2047, Justice Hollins had before her this question: if a party objects to making an admission which is sought, must that party provide grounds for the objection?
Her Ladyship said: [26] … Rule 6.37(2)(b)(ii) can only fulfil its objective if the basis for the objection—which is wholly within the knowledge of the responding party - is disclosed.
Without it, there is no discernible purpose or intention to the Rule; Rule 1.7(1).
[27] In my view, an objection to an admission sought must:
(1) delineate whether the objection is because the admission sought is irrelevant, improper or unnecessary; and
(2) offer a basic reason for why that is so, in the view of the responding party.
Many of the possibilities have been seen in other cases.

For example, in Andriuk, the following bases for objections were identified: ambiguity, generality, legal determinations, conclusory statements that lack a foundation, improper form and opinions on highly specialized subjects.

In Canada Southern Petroleum Ltd v Amoco Canada Petroleum Co, 1994 CarswellAlta 716 O’Leary, J (as he then was) also listed a number of possible responses that could be proper objections e.g. lack of independent knowledge, requiring the interpretation of a document or a legal conclusion, a document that speaks for itself or a request that is too vague to answer; paras.10-14.
Her Ladyship’s reference to “Rule 6.37(2)(b)(ii)” would seem to be an inadvertent error.
The Rule referred to is Rule 6.37(3)((b)(ii).
Costs The plaintiff asks for additional costs because the defendant failed to admit two facts when given the opportunity to do so in answer to a notice to admit.
The notice to admit process is provided in the Rules in an effort to shorten trials and thereby make them less costly.

When a litigant wrongly fails to admit a fact which it has been requested to admit, and where the originating party is then put to the trouble and expense of calling evidence to prove the fact in issue, the originating party is entitled to costs in relation to that evidence.

Where the originating party is also the successful party, that party is entitled to additional costs to reflect the time and trouble of calling the disputed evidence, even though the originating party will get costs that include all the time taken for the trial.
This is because the tariff only compensates the successful party for a portion of the costs expended on the trial.
Additional compensation can, and should, be awarded where appropriate.
Waterous Investments Inc. v.
Liberton Holdings Ltd.
229 (Q.B.), at 235, per Veit J.
In Ellis v.
Friedland (2000), 276 A.R.

364 (Q.B.), the defendant, having been successful at trial, sought “increased costs because the plaintiff did not admit substantial and material facts as stated in the defendant's Notices to Admit, and such facts were later proven at trial.” In other words, the defendant was seeking costs in excess of those incurred in proving the fact which should have been admitted.
McMahon J. considered Rule 230(4), and, in denying the application for additional costs, said, at p.
367: It is clear that the penalty for an unreasonable refusal to admit facts is payment of costs for proving that matter.
There is no provision in R.
230(4) for increasing a costs award.
In Patterson v.
Hryciuk, 2005 ABQB 136, 2005 CarswellAlta 309, 45 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 240, at pp.

250-251, Macklin J. said the following concerning the award of costs for facts not admitted after service of a Notice to Admit: The service of a Notice to Admit Facts is not a procedure to be invoked by a party in an attempt to increase its potential costs award in the same manner as the compromise procedures set out in Part 12 of the Rules.
The purpose of a Notice to Admit Facts is to try and expedite the trial procedure and minimize or reduce costs by obviating the necessity of calling certain evidence.

Where the evidence necessary to be called is going to be called in any event and the requested admissions can be given in evidence with minimal or no additional time or expense involved, it is inappropriate to try and use the rule to invoke cost penalties in an attempt to increase the potential costs award following trial.

Rule Applies to Civil Judicial Review Applications It is the conclusion of this Court that the procedure stipulated in Rule 230 is available to the Applicant in the present civil judicial review application.
Consideration by the Court of the applicability of any of the general rules to a judicial review procedure must first begin with a consideration of those rules themselves.

Rule 753.19 specifically directs the applicability of all general rules to judicial review matters unless otherwise “provided specificially in that part.” There is no special provision excluding Rule 230 in Part 56.1.

When considering the application of any interlocutory procedural rule to judicial review applications, the Court is also entitled to consider the objectives behind the implementation of the new judicial review procedures… In principle, technical objections to the applicablility of the general rules are to be discouraged… In the Alberta Rules, the use of the Notice relates to any “cause, matter or issue”.
A proceeding for judicial review is to be commenced by Originating Notice in Alberta.
By definition that is a document by which an action is initiated.
Surely there can be no meaningful distinction between [an]“action” and “cause, matter or issue.” . . . . .
There appears to this Court no apparent practical reason for excluding the use of this procedure in such a case as this.
There may be some situations of judicial review in which Rule 230 ought not to be available.
Certainly, the scope for its use where the judicial review is based on alleged error within the jurisdiction of a lower tribunal or officer on the face of the record would appear to be limited.
Alberta River Conservation Foundation v.
Alberta (Minister of Environmental Protection) (1998), 58 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 287 (Q.B.), at 292-94, per Wilkins J.

paragraphs.text: (1) On application, the Court may order a person to attend for questioning at a date, time and place specified by the Court, if the person (a) is required to be questioned under these rules, (b) was served with a notice of appointment for questioning in Form 29 under these rules, (c) was provided with an allowance, determined in accordance with Schedule B, if so required by these rules, and (d) did not attend the appointment, attended the appointment but refused to answer or fully answer proper questions or did not bring a record required to be brought to the questioning. paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 6.40 – Part 6. Resolving Issues And Preserving Rights
paragraphs.text: (1) The Court may appoint a person as a court expert to give evidence on a matter. (2) The court expert must give independent evidence to the Court. (3) If possible, the parties must agree on the court expert to be appointed under subrule (1). (4) The appointment of a court expert does not affect the right of a party to call the party's own expert as a witness. (5) If the court expert is a health care professional, the court expert has all the authority and responsibility conferred on a health care professional by these rules.
